raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old man, nonsmoker, without past medical history especially personal or family history of inherited immunodeficiency disorders or autoimmune diseases, was admitted to the hospital complaining of hemoptysis, dyspnea on exertion, fever, weight, and appetite loss for 45 days. On examination, the patient was febrile at 38.5 C and hypoxemic (Oxygen saturation on a nasal cannula at 1 L was 91%). The chest X-ray revealed bilateral and extensive alveolar opacities (Figure 1).
Laboratory results indicated the presence of inflammatory syndrome (white blood cell: 11,800/mm3, C-reactive protein: 220 mg/L), hemoglobin: 11.7 g/dL, hepatic cytolysis, and cholestasis. Sputum and blood culture did not yield any organisms. Serology for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, and Chlamydia pneumoniae were negative. Pneumococcal antigen urinary testing was negative. The HIV antibody test was negative. Serum rheumatoid factor was positive (64 UI/mL). Antinuclear antibodies, anti-cyclical Citrullinated Peptide antibodies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative.
The lymphocyte subpopulations CD4, CD8, and CD4/CD8 were carried out and were normal (1050/mm3, 480/mm3, 2.18%, respectively) .The serum levels of immunoglobulin M, G, and A were within the normal ranges (1.7 g/L, 12 g/L, 2.3 g/L, respectively).
Computed tomography (CT) (Figure 2) revealed multiple diffuse consolidations associated with nodules sometimes displaying necrosis, along with enlarged necrotized bilateral mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes and pericardial effusion.
The patient was treated with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid 1 g x 3 daily for 7 days. On the fifth day, bronchoscopy with bronchial aspiration was performed for cytology, BK testing, and bacteriological examination, and it was normal. The bacteriological study of bronchial fluid has been performed, excluding specific testing for Pneumocystis. Both direct examination and culture were unable to identify any microorganisms. Dyspnea escalated (relying on 5 L per minute with a high-concentration mask and subsequently necessitating noninvasive ventilation due to hypercapnia), while the fever remained. The chest film showed an extension of alveolar opacities (Figure 3). Inflammatory syndrome increased (white blood cell: 16,800/mm3, C-reactive protein: 343 mg/L). Antibiotic therapy switched to imipenem 1 g x 3 daily, vancomycin 1 g x 2 daily for 12 days for both, and levofloxacin 500 mg x 2 daily for 2 days, then 500 mg daily for 10 days.
A second bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and protected distal sampling was conducted due to ongoing fever and the advancement of alveolar opacities. It revealed inflammation throughout the entire bronchial tree mucosa. The protected distal sampling showed a polymorphic pattern. Bronchial biopsy showed an inflammatory mucosa. The bronchial fluid was examined by optic microscopy. It contained inflammatory but not neoplastic cells. A study of bronchial fluid by Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) on cellblock revealed a few Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms (Figure 4(a) and 4(b)).
The diagnosis of PCP was established. The patient was, therefore, treated with oral Sulfamethoxazole-Trimethoprim 1600 mg per day in four doses and dexamethasone 40 mg twice per day (which was gradually tapered off) for 3 weeks.
The patient exhibited clinical improvement (afebrile, oxygen saturation: 95% on room air) and biological improvement (white blood cell count: 14,000/mm3, C-reactive protein: 23 mg/L). He was discharged home without complications.
The patient was seen at the outpatient clinic 1 month after discharge from the hospital, and he reported no respiratory complaints. Subsequently, he was lost to follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A previously healthy 42-year-old nonsmoking man presented with a 45-day history of hemoptysis, exertional dyspnea, fever, weight loss, and anorexia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had no known medical comorbidities or immunodeficiency risk factors, developed progressive hemoptysis, dyspnea on exertion, fever, loss of appetite, and weight loss over 45 days prior to hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable; nonsmoker with no personal or family history of inherited immunodeficiency disorders or autoimmune diseases.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for hemoptysis, exertional dyspnea, fever, weight loss, and loss of appetite.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: Febrile with body temperature 38.5 °C and hypoxemic with SpO2 91% on 1 L/min nasal cannula oxygen.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory tests: WBC 11,800/mm3 (later rising to 16,800/mm3), C-reactive protein (CRP) 220 mg/L (later rising to 343 mg/L), hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, and elevated liver transaminases/cholestatic enzymes (hepatic cytolysis and cholestasis). Microbiological screening: Sputum and blood cultures negative; serologies for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, and Chlamydia pneumoniae negative; urinary pneumococcal antigen negative; HIV antibody test negative. Autoimmune and immunoglobulin panel: Positive serum rheumatoid factor (64 IU/mL); negative ANA, anti-CCP, and ANCA; normal serum IgM (1.7 g/L), IgG (12 g/L), and IgA (2.3 g/L). Chest X-ray: Extensive bilateral alveolar opacities (which extended further during initial empirical antibiotic therapy).
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline lymphocyte subsets: Normal CD4 count (1,050/mm3), CD8 count (480/mm3), and CD4/CD8 ratio (2.18). Chest CT: Multiple diffuse consolidations associated with variably necrotic pulmonary nodules, enlarged necrotic bilateral mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, and pericardial effusion. First bronchoscopy (day 5): Normal bronchial aspiration cytology, acid-fast (BK) testing, and routine bacteriology (Pneumocystis stain not initially performed). Second bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), protected distal sampling, and bronchial biopsy: Diffuse bronchial mucosal inflammation without neoplastic cells; Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining on the bronchial fluid cellblock identified Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) in an immunocompetent, HIV-negative adult with normal CD4+ T-cell counts (1,050/mm3), confirmed by Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) staining on bronchoalveolar lavage cellblock. Plan and clinical course: The patient initially failed 7 days of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (1 g TID) and 12 days of broad-spectrum escalation to imipenem (1 g TID), vancomycin (1 g BID), and levofloxacin (500 mg BID for 2 days, then 500 mg daily), during which his dyspnea progressed to require a 5 L/min high-concentration mask and noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnia. Following GMS confirmation of P. jirovecii on the second bronchoscopy, he was treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (1,600 mg/day divided in four doses) and dexamethasone (40 mg twice daily, gradually tapered) for 3 weeks. He achieved full clinical recovery (afebrile, SpO2 95% on room air) and inflammatory improvement (WBC 14,000/mm3, CRP 23 mg/L), was discharged home without complications, and remained asymptomatic at 1-month outpatient follow-up.
